en: The Philippine eagle has a shaggy crest and hunts monkeys and colugos in the tall forest canopy of Mindanao.
The endemic Philippine Jade Vine produces striking turquoise flowers that hang downward to attract nectar-feeding bat pollinators.
Bangus, or milkfish, hatch in the ocean but migrate to shallow coastal lagoons and fishponds to grow.
Filipinos eat ampalaya, or bitter melon, because its compounds help lower blood sugar levels in the human body.
The tiny Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes and can rotate its head almost completely around to spot nighttime insects.
Abaca plants, native to the Philippines, yield strong fibers from their leaf stalks to weave ropes and paper.
The critically endangered Tamaraw, a dwarf buffalo endemic to Mindoro, survives by grazing on grass in mountain forests.
Vitamin C from Philippine guava helps the human immune system produce white blood cells to fight bacterial infections.
The Philippine pitcher plant digests trapped insects inside specialized, fluid-filled leaves to absorb nitrogen in nutrient-poor mountain soils.
The carabao, or water buffalo, has sparse hair and wallows in mud to regulate its body temperature during hot summers.
The Banaue Rice Terraces create a unique ecosystem where water flows from mountain forests to irrigate stepped rice paddies.
The freshwater Philippine crocodile uses its camouflaged, scaly skin to hide underwater and ambush fish in Mindanao's lakes.
